title: Reproductive Endocrine Conditions: Amenorrhea, Anovulation, Abnormal Bleeding, and Ovarian Failure
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)

overview.intro: This chapter applies the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis to the menstrual disorders that arise from hormones rather than from infection or tumor. It covers amenorrhea and how FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, and estradiol localize it; anovulation and the unopposed estrogen that follows; abnormal uterine bleeding; menopause and primary ovarian insufficiency; androgen excess; menstrual pain; and the main categories of female infertility. Board questions usually give a short history with a hormone panel and ask where the defect lies or what a hormone change will do to the endometrium, bone, or vessels. If you can trace each finding to a broken feedback loop, these questions become predictable.
prerequisites: Hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis: pulsatile GnRH, FSH, LH, estradiol, inhibin, and progesterone feedback
Follicular, ovulatory, and luteal phases of the ovarian cycle and proliferative and secretory endometrium
Steroidogenesis in theca, granulosa, and adrenal cortex, including aromatase and 21-hydroxylase
Mullerian duct development and the anatomy of the uterus, tubes, and vagina
Prolactin regulation by dopamine and TRH

connections.how: Prolactinomas, hypothyroidism, Sheehan syndrome, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia all present as menstrual disorders.
Estrogen restrains RANKL-driven osteoclast activity, so every low-estrogen state in this chapter causes bone loss.
Unopposed estrogen leads to endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid carcinoma, and leiomyomas and adenomyosis are the structural mimics of hormonal bleeding.
Chlamydia and gonorrhea scar the fallopian tubes, which is the mechanism of tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

connections.to: Genetics (sex chromosome and triplet repeat disorders)
connections.how: Turner syndrome, androgen insensitivity, and the FMR1 premutation explain several causes of amenorrhea and early ovarian failure.

terms.def: Absence of menstruation, classed as primary (menses never started) or secondary (menses stopped after starting).
A cycle in which no oocyte is released, so no corpus luteum forms and no progesterone is made.
Estrogen stimulation of the endometrium without the progesterone that normally converts it to secretory tissue and limits growth.
Low ovarian steroid output with high FSH and LH because the ovary has failed and feedback is lost.
Low ovarian steroid output with low or inappropriately normal FSH and LH because the hypothalamus or pituitary has failed.
Intrauterine adhesions after injury to the basal endometrium, usually from curettage, causing amenorrhea or light menses with normal hormones.
The FIGO classification of abnormal uterine bleeding into structural causes (PALM) and nonstructural causes (COEIN).
Permanent cessation of menses from follicle depletion, diagnosed after 12 months without menses.
Loss of normal ovarian function before age 40, with high FSH and low estradiol.
Excess terminal hair in a male pattern in a woman, from androgen excess or increased follicle sensitivity to androgens.
Masculinization beyond hair growth, such as clitoromegaly, voice deepening, and temporal balding, which implies high androgen levels.
Unilateral lower abdominal pain at midcycle related to ovulation.

blocks.text: Regular menses require an intact chain: pulsatile GnRH from the hypothalamus drives FSH and LH, the ovary responds with follicle growth and estradiol, ovulation produces a corpus luteum that secretes progesterone, and the fall of progesterone at the end of the luteal phase sheds the endometrium through an open cervix and vagina. A break anywhere in that chain stops menstruation, and the two definitions of amenorrhea simply describe when the break appeared.

Primary amenorrhea is no menarche by age 15 in a person with normal secondary sexual characteristics, or no menarche by age 13 when breast development has not begun. The earlier cutoff exists because absent breast development at 13 already shows that estrogen has never been adequate. Secondary amenorrhea is the absence of menses for 3 months in someone who previously had regular cycles, or for 6 months if cycles were irregular.

Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea, and it can also present as primary amenorrhea if conception occurs before the first period, so hCG is always the first test. In pregnancy, hCG from the trophoblast acts on the LH receptor to keep the corpus luteum secreting progesterone, so the lining never undergoes withdrawal shedding.
Using the physical examination as a bioassay

Two findings sort primary amenorrhea quickly. Breast development (thelarche) proves that the gonads made estrogen at some point. A normal uterus on examination or ultrasound proves that Mullerian ducts formed, which also means anti-Mullerian hormone from testes was absent during development. Pubic and axillary hair reflect androgen action and help separate the two conditions in which breasts are present but the uterus is missing.

blocks.title: Primary amenorrhea by breast development and uterus
rows: Gonadal dysgenesis such as Turner syndrome or 46,XY Swyer syndrome (high FSH); Kallmann syndrome or constitutional delay (low FSH)
No estrogen; FSH level separates ovarian failure from central failure
Mullerian agenesis (46,XX, normal pubic hair); complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY, scant pubic hair)
Mullerian ducts failed to form, or testes made AMH; in androgen insensitivity, testosterone is aromatized to estradiol
Imperforate hymen or transverse vaginal septum; otherwise evaluate as for secondary amenorrhea
Outflow obstruction gives cyclic pelvic pain and trapped blood (hematocolpos)
Rare 46,XY states: testicular regression after AMH has acted, or 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency
Testes made AMH, so ducts regressed, but no estrogen was produced
blocks.caption: Gonadal dysgenesis is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea and Mullerian agenesis the second most common.

blocks.text: Kallmann syndrome deserves special mention because its mechanism is developmental: GnRH neurons arise in the olfactory placode and migrate into the hypothalamus with olfactory axons. When that migration fails, the result is GnRH deficiency with anosmia or hyposmia, low FSH and LH, and absent puberty. Secondary amenorrhea, by contrast, is usually acquired: pregnancy, functional hypothalamic suppression, PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease, ovarian insufficiency, and intrauterine adhesions account for most cases, and the next section shows how hormones sort them.

blocks.predict: A 16 year old has normal breast development, sparse pubic and axillary hair, and a blind-ending vagina with no palpable uterus. What is her karyotype likely to be, and why are the breasts normal?
blocks.explain: Androgen insensitivity in a 46,XY person: testes secrete AMH, so Mullerian structures regress, and testosterone that cannot act is aromatized to estradiol, which develops the breasts. Sparse hair reflects absent androgen action.
blocks.check: Compare with the second row of the primary amenorrhea table and the paragraph on the physical examination as a bioassay.

sections.title: Localizing amenorrhea with FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, and estradiol

blocks.text: Once pregnancy is excluded, the hormone panel locates the break in the axis by applying one rule of negative feedback. Estradiol and inhibin B from the ovary hold FSH and LH down. If the ovary fails, the brake is released and gonadotropins rise, so high FSH with low estradiol (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) places the defect in the ovary. If the hypothalamus or pituitary fails, the ovary is simply unstimulated, so FSH, LH, and estradiol are all low, or gonadotropins are inappropriately normal for the low estradiol (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism).

Prolactin and TSH are measured with FSH because both cause central suppression. Prolactin inhibits pulsatile GnRH release, acting largely through hypothalamic kisspeptin neurons, so hyperprolactinemia from a prolactinoma, from dopamine antagonist drugs, or from stalk compression lowers FSH and LH. In primary hypothyroidism, raised TRH stimulates lactotrophs as well as thyrotrophs, so prolactin rises and menses stop; correcting the thyroid deficit corrects the prolactin.

blocks.title: Hormone patterns that localize amenorrhea
rows: Low energy availability, weight loss, stress, anosmia
High prolactin, mass effect, postpartum hemorrhage with failure to lactate
Primary ovarian insufficiency, Turner syndrome, menopause
Cyclic hormonal symptoms but no bleeding
blocks.caption: PCOS usually shows normal FSH, normal or raised LH, normal estradiol, and raised androgens, so it does not fit the low-estrogen rows.

blocks.title: Classic stepwise evaluation of secondary amenorrhea
steps: Negative hCG excludes pregnancy
Measure TSH and prolactin for central suppression
Progestin challenge: bleeding means estrogen present and outflow open
No bleed: give estrogen then progestin
Still no bleed: outflow tract defect such as Asherman syndrome
Bleed after estrogen: hypoestrogenic, so FSH separates ovary from brain
blocks.caption: The progestin and estrogen challenges test, in order, whether the endometrium is estrogen primed and whether the outflow tract can respond at all.

blocks.text: Asherman syndrome is the outflow defect boards favor. Vigorous curettage, especially of a recently pregnant uterus, or endometrial infection, destroys the stratum basalis, the layer that regenerates the functionalis each cycle. Fibrous adhesions then bridge the cavity. Because the ovary and pituitary are untouched, FSH, LH, and estradiol are normal, ovulation continues, and the patient may notice cyclic breast or mood changes without bleeding; the endometrium simply cannot respond.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a hormone panel
blocks.text: A 27 year old marathon runner with a body mass index of 17 kg/m2 has had no menses for 8 months. hCG is negative, TSH and prolactin are normal, FSH and LH are low normal, and estradiol is low. Step 1: low estradiol means the endometrium is not being built, so a progestin challenge would produce little or no bleeding. Step 2: if the ovary had failed, FSH would be high; it is not, so the ovary is unstimulated rather than broken. Step 3: normal prolactin and TSH exclude the two common pituitary-level suppressors. Step 4: low energy availability, with low leptin and stress-related CRH, slows GnRH pulses. The defect is hypothalamic, and the low estradiol predicts bone loss.

sections.title: Anovulation and the consequences of unopposed estrogen

blocks.text: Ovulation depends on a switch in estradiol feedback. Early in the follicular phase, estradiol suppresses FSH and LH. When the dominant follicle raises estradiol above about 200 pg/mL and holds it there for about 2 days, the hypothalamus and pituitary switch to positive feedback, GnRH pulses and pituitary sensitivity rise, and the LH surge follows. Ovulation occurs about 34 to 36 hours after the surge begins. Anovulation results when this sequence fails, either because no follicle matures enough to deliver the estradiol signal, or because the estradiol signal arrives but the hypothalamus cannot respond with a surge.

blocks.title: Causes of anovulation and their mechanisms
rows: Fast GnRH pulses favor LH; LH and insulin drive theca androgen; relative FSH lack arrests follicles
Prolactin slows GnRH pulses, lowering FSH and LH
High TRH raises prolactin; altered SHBG and steroid clearance disturb feedback
Raised SHBG and altered steroid metabolism disrupt cycles, often with light or absent menses
Low leptin, raised cortisol, and reduced kisspeptin slow GnRH pulses
Physiologic: first years after menarche, perimenopause
Immature positive feedback or failing follicle supply
blocks.caption: Only causes that leave estrogen present produce the unopposed estrogen effects; severe hypothalamic suppression instead produces low estrogen and bone loss.

blocks.text: Why PCOS is self-sustaining

In PCOS, more frequent GnRH pulses favor LH over FSH. LH stimulates theca cells to make androstenedione and testosterone, and insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia amplifies theca androgen output and suppresses hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), raising free testosterone. Granulosa cells, short of FSH-driven aromatase, cannot convert the androgen load, and the local androgen excess arrests follicles at the small antral stage, producing many small follicles. Androstenedione is aromatized to estrone in adipose tissue, giving a steady, acyclic estrogen level that never rises sharply enough to trigger a surge.

blocks.title: The PCOS loop
steps: Rapid GnRH pulses raise LH relative to FSH
LH and insulin increase theca androgen
Follicles arrest; no dominant follicle, no LH surge
Adipose aromatization gives steady acyclic estrone
Acyclic estrogen and low progesterone keep GnRH pulses rapid
blocks.caption: Without a luteal phase, progesterone never slows GnRH pulse frequency, so the LH predominance persists.

blocks.text: Unopposed estrogen

Without ovulation there is no corpus luteum and therefore no progesterone. Progesterone normally converts proliferative endometrium to secretory endometrium, reduces estrogen receptor expression, and induces 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, which converts estradiol to the weaker estrone. When estrogen acts without that brake, the endometrium keeps proliferating. Clinically this gives irregular cycles with intervals of amenorrhea punctuated by heavy, prolonged bleeding, described in the next section. Over months to years the glands crowd and proliferate abnormally, producing endometrial hyperplasia. Hyperplasia with atypia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia) is the direct precursor of endometrioid (type I) endometrial carcinoma, which is why obesity, PCOS, and estrogen-only exposure share the same cancer risk.

blocks.predict: Why does a woman with PCOS have a higher risk of endometrial carcinoma than a woman with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, even though both are anovulatory?
blocks.explain: In PCOS, estrogen is present but never opposed by progesterone, so the endometrium proliferates continuously. In hypothalamic amenorrhea, estrogen itself is low, so the endometrium is thin and inactive.
blocks.check: Compare the estrogen status column of the anovulation table with the paragraph on unopposed estrogen.

sections.title: Anovulatory bleeding (AUB-O) versus structural causes of abnormal uterine bleeding

blocks.text: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding is the older name for bleeding caused by ovulatory dysfunction. In the current FIGO PALM-COEIN classification it is called abnormal uterine bleeding from ovulatory dysfunction (AUB-O), and it is diagnosed only after structural causes, pregnancy, and coagulopathy have been excluded.

Normal menstruation is orderly because it is a progesterone withdrawal event. When the corpus luteum regresses, the fall in progesterone triggers prostaglandin release, spiral arteriole vasoconstriction, and ischemia of the whole functionalis at once. The layer sheds synchronously down to the basalis, and platelet plugs and vasoconstriction stop the bleeding within about 4 to 7 days. In AUB-O, a thick estrogen-driven endometrium without secretory change outgrows its stromal and vascular support. Fragile, dilated vessels break down in patches at different times, so shedding is asynchronous: some areas bleed while others are still proliferating. The result is irregular timing, unpredictable volume, and often prolonged heavy bleeding (estrogen breakthrough bleeding). A fall in estrogen, as when a follicle undergoes atresia, can also trigger bleeding (estrogen withdrawal bleeding). Biopsy shows proliferative or disordered proliferative endometrium with no secretory change, or hyperplasia.

blocks.title: PALM-COEIN classification of abnormal uterine bleeding
rows: Localized overgrowth of endometrium with thick-walled vessels; intermenstrual or postmenopausal spotting
Endometrial glands and stroma within myometrium; enlarged, globular, tender uterus with heavy painful menses
Benign smooth muscle tumor; submucosal myomas enlarge and distort the cavity and impair contraction, causing heavy menses
Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma; postmenopausal bleeding requires exclusion of carcinoma
von Willebrand disease is the classic inherited cause; heavy bleeding since menarche
Anovulation with unopposed estrogen; irregular, unpredictable bleeding
Primary disorder of local hemostasis or inflammation in an ovulatory woman
Rare or poorly defined entities such as arteriovenous malformation
blocks.caption: Structural causes can be seen on imaging or histology; nonstructural causes cannot.

blocks.text: The pattern of bleeding helps separate the groups. Ovulatory dysfunction produces irregular cycles because the timing of shedding no longer follows a luteal phase. Structural lesions usually leave ovulation intact, so cycles stay regular but menses become heavier (leiomyoma, adenomyosis) or spotting appears between them (polyp). Postmenopausal bleeding is a separate red flag: atrophy is its most common cause, but endometrial carcinoma must be excluded because unopposed estrogen from adipose aromatization and hyperplasia are common in this age group.

sections.title: Menopause and the effects of estrogen loss

blocks.text: A woman is born with about 1 to 2 million oocytes, about 300,000 to 400,000 remain at puberty, and atresia continues throughout life, so only a few hundred are ever ovulated. Menopause occurs when the follicle pool falls below the number needed to sustain cycles, at an average age of about 51 years in the United States. It is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months without menses. Perimenopause (the menopausal transition) is the preceding period of irregular cycles.

The first hormonal change is a fall in inhibin B, which granulosa cells of small antral follicles secrete in proportion to their number. Losing inhibin removes selective negative feedback on FSH, so FSH rises in the early follicular phase while estradiol is still normal or even high. Faster follicle recruitment shortens cycles at first; later, cycles lengthen and become anovulatory, which is why perimenopause brings irregular, sometimes heavy, bleeding. After the final follicles are gone, estradiol and progesterone fall, both negative feedback signals are lost, and FSH and LH rise, with FSH rising more than LH. The ovarian stroma continues to secrete androgens, and estrone from adipose aromatization becomes the main circulating estrogen.

blocks.title: Feedback changes from perimenopause to menopause
steps: Follicle pool shrinks
Inhibin B falls; early FSH rise
Cycles shorten, then become anovulatory
Estradiol and inhibin A also fall
FSH and LH remain high; estrone from fat dominates
blocks.caption: FSH rises first and most because it alone is controlled by inhibin as well as estradiol.

blocks.title: Effects of estrogen loss and their mechanisms
rows: Loss of estrogen feedback enlarges hypothalamic KNDy (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, dynorphin) neurons; increased neurokinin B signaling narrows the thermoneutral zone, so small rises in core temperature trigger vasodilation and sweating
Thin vaginal epithelium stores less glycogen; fewer lactobacilli make less lactic acid, pH rises above about 4.5, causing dryness, dyspareunia, and recurrent urinary infection
Estrogen normally lowers RANKL and raises osteoprotegerin and induces osteoclast apoptosis; its loss increases osteoclast number and lifespan, with the fastest trabecular bone loss in the first years
LDL rises and HDL falls, and loss of estrogen-stimulated endothelial nitric oxide synthase reduces vasodilation
blocks.caption: Each consequence follows from loss of a specific estrogen action, so the same list applies to any hypoestrogenic state.

blocks.text: Elevated FSH confirms the diagnosis biochemically but is not required in a woman over 45 with typical symptoms, because FSH fluctuates widely during the transition. A woman under 40 with the same profile has primary ovarian insufficiency, described next.

blocks.predict: In early perimenopause, why can FSH be raised while estradiol is still normal?
blocks.explain: Inhibin B falls first as the antral follicle pool shrinks. Losing inhibin removes the FSH-specific brake before estradiol output declines.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on the first hormonal change and the feedback flow.

blocks.text: Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), also called premature ovarian failure, is loss of ovarian function before age 40. It affects about 1% of women. It is defined by at least 4 months of oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea with FSH above about 25 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart, and estradiol is low. Unlike menopause, POI is often intermittent: some women ovulate occasionally and a small minority conceive, which is why the term insufficiency replaced failure.

The hormone profile is the same as menopause for the same reason: depleted or nonfunctioning follicles make little estradiol and inhibin, so negative feedback is lost and FSH and LH rise. Anti-Mullerian hormone, made by granulosa cells of small growing follicles, is low or undetectable and reflects the shrunken pool. The consequences of hypoestrogenism, including vasomotor symptoms, vaginal atrophy, bone loss, and greater cardiovascular risk, arrive years earlier than in natural menopause.

blocks.title: Causes of primary ovarian insufficiency
rows: Two X chromosomes are needed to maintain oocytes; accelerated atresia leaves streak gonads, so most present with primary amenorrhea, while mosaics may menstruate briefly
Premutation mRNA is toxic to follicles; a minority of carriers, about 20%, develop POI; the full mutation causing fragile X syndrome does not
Lymphocytic attack on steroid-producing theca cells of growing follicles; often with autoimmune adrenal insufficiency and steroid cell or 21-hydroxylase antibodies
Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and ionizing radiation destroy oocytes; risk rises with dose and with age
Galactose metabolites are toxic to the developing ovary
No cause found in most cases
blocks.caption: A karyotype and FMR1 testing are part of the evaluation because Turner mosaicism and premutation carriers are otherwise easily missed.

blocks.text: Two distinctions are tested. POI is hypergonadotropic, whereas the low-estrogen amenorrhea of hypothalamic suppression is hypogonadotropic, so FSH separates them. And autoimmune POI should prompt thought about the adrenal, because adrenal autoimmunity often travels with it and untreated adrenal insufficiency is dangerous.

sections.title: Hirsutism, virilization, and localizing androgen excess

blocks.text: Hirsutism is excess terminal hair in a male pattern (upper lip, chin, chest, linea alba, back, inner thighs) in a woman. It occurs when androgens convert fine vellus hairs into coarse pigmented terminal hairs, which depends both on androgen level and on follicle sensitivity, largely through local 5-alpha-reductase conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone. Hirsutism alone indicates mild to moderate androgen excess. Virilization means masculinization beyond hair: clitoromegaly, voice deepening, increased muscle mass, temporal balding, and loss of female body contour. It requires much higher androgen levels, so rapid onset of virilization suggests an androgen-secreting tumor until proven otherwise.

Localizing the source depends on where each androgen is made. In women, about a quarter of testosterone comes directly from the ovary, about a quarter from the adrenal, and about half from peripheral conversion of androstenedione that both glands secrete. Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S), by contrast, comes almost entirely from the adrenal zona reticularis, which secretes DHEA largely in its sulfated form. Testosterone therefore reflects total androgen production, while DHEA-S is an adrenal marker.

blocks.title: Localizing androgen excess
rows: Gradual onset from puberty, irregular cycles, insulin resistance
Raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone, rising further after ACTH stimulation
Rapid onset, may also secrete cortisol
blocks.caption: High testosterone with normal DHEA-S points to the ovary; high DHEA-S points to the adrenal.

blocks.text: In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, cortisol synthesis is impaired, ACTH rises, and the accumulated 17-hydroxyprogesterone is diverted into the androgen pathway. The classic form virilizes a female fetus; the nonclassic form appears after puberty and closely mimics PCOS, which is why 17-hydroxyprogesterone is measured. PCOS remains the most common cause of hirsutism and is diagnosed by the Rotterdam criteria (two of three: ovulatory dysfunction, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology) after excluding other causes.

blocks.title: Worked example: ovary or adrenal?
blocks.text: A 34 year old has 5 months of worsening facial hair, a deepening voice, and clitoromegaly. Total testosterone is 260 ng/dL, DHEA-S is normal, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone is normal. Step 1: voice change and clitoromegaly are virilization, not simple hirsutism, so androgen levels must be very high, and the short history suggests a tumor. Step 2: testosterone far above about 150 to 200 ng/dL fits a tumor rather than PCOS. Step 3: normal DHEA-S argues against an adrenal source, and normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone excludes CAH. Step 4: the source is ovarian, most classically a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, and imaging should look for an adnexal mass.

Primary dysmenorrhea is painful menstruation without pelvic disease. It usually begins within a year or two after menarche, once cycles become ovulatory, because the mechanism requires a luteal phase followed by progesterone withdrawal. Pain is crampy, lower midline, and may radiate to the back and thighs; it starts with or just before the flow and lasts about 1 to 3 days.

Progesterone stabilizes lysosomal membranes in endometrial cells. When it falls, phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid, and cyclooxygenase converts it to prostaglandin F2-alpha and prostaglandin E2. Women with dysmenorrhea have higher endometrial and menstrual fluid prostaglandin levels. PGF2-alpha raises resting myometrial tone and the strength and frequency of contractions, and the contractions compress vessels, so the myometrium becomes ischemic, much as exercising muscle does when its blood supply is limited. Prostaglandins also sensitize pain fibers, and when they enter the circulation they cause the nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and headache that often accompany cramps. The relief produced by cyclooxygenase inhibitors confirms this mechanism.

blocks.title: Mechanism of primary dysmenorrhea
steps: Corpus luteum regresses; progesterone falls
Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid
COX produces PGF2-alpha and PGE2
Myometrial hypercontractility and vasoconstriction
Ischemia and sensitized nerve endings cause pain
blocks.caption: Anovulatory cycles lack the progesterone withdrawal step, which is why the earliest cycles after menarche are often painless.

blocks.text: Secondary dysmenorrhea comes from pelvic pathology such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, or leiomyoma. Clues are onset years after menarche, pain that worsens over time or begins before menses, dyspareunia, heavy bleeding, and an abnormal pelvic examination.
Mittelschmerz

Mittelschmerz is unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain at midcycle, about 14 days before the next menses, on the side of the ovulating ovary, so it may switch sides from month to month. It lasts from minutes to a day or two. The pain is attributed to stretching of the ovarian capsule by the enlarging follicle just before rupture and to peritoneal irritation by follicular fluid or a small amount of blood released at rupture. Its importance for boards is diagnostic: right-sided mittelschmerz can mimic appendicitis, and timing in the cycle, a negative pregnancy test (to exclude ectopic pregnancy), and the absence of fever help separate them.

sections.title: Ovulatory, tubal, and uterine causes of female infertility

blocks.text: Infertility is failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse, shortened to 6 months for women 35 or older because fecundity falls with age. Conception requires a released oocyte, an open tube where sperm and oocyte meet and the embryo is transported, and a receptive endometrium for implantation; female infertility can be grouped by which of these fails. Male factors contribute in a large share of couples and are evaluated in parallel.

blocks.title: Female infertility by category
rows: PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, hypothalamic amenorrhea, primary ovarian insufficiency, thyroid disease
No LH surge or no follicles, so no oocyte is released
Prior pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, prior pelvic surgery
Scarred, blocked, or deciliated tubes prevent gamete meeting and embryo transport
Asherman syndrome, submucosal leiomyoma, Mullerian anomalies such as uterine septum
Cavity is obliterated or distorted, so implantation fails or pregnancy is lost
blocks.caption: Ovulatory disorders are the most readily identified group; PCOS is their most common cause.

blocks.text: Ovulatory infertility

Each ovulatory cause works through mechanisms already described: PCOS and hyperprolactinemia prevent a dominant follicle and LH surge, low energy availability slows GnRH pulses, and ovarian insufficiency leaves no follicles to recruit. Ovulation can be confirmed biochemically by a mid-luteal serum progesterone above about 3 ng/mL, which shows that a corpus luteum formed. Regular cycles of 21 to 35 days with premenstrual symptoms also suggest ovulation.
Tubal infertility

Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae ascend from the cervix to cause salpingitis. Chlamydia in particular can be silent while inducing a chronic immune response that damages ciliated epithelium and mucosal folds, and repair produces fibrosis, fimbrial adhesions, and distal occlusion with a fluid-filled hydrosalpinx. Partly damaged tubes may still admit sperm yet fail to move the embryo, so the same scarring raises the risk of ectopic pregnancy. Each additional episode of pelvic inflammatory disease increases the risk. Hysterosalpingography shows whether contrast flows through the tubes.
Uterine infertility

In Asherman syndrome, adhesions replace the functionalis and leave little or no endometrium able to undergo decidualization, so implantation fails or early pregnancy is lost. Submucosal leiomyomas project into the cavity, distort its shape, and alter the overlying endometrium and its blood flow, which lowers implantation rates; intramural and subserosal myomas affect fertility much less. These are the same lesions that cause outflow-type amenorrhea and structural abnormal bleeding, which ties infertility back to the earlier sections.

integration.text: The conditions in this chapter are best understood as failures at different levels of one feedback loop. Anatomy and embryology explain the outflow and Mullerian causes, from imperforate hymen to Asherman syndrome. Physiology explains why FSH rises when the ovary fails but falls when the brain fails, and why estrogen without progesterone overstimulates the endometrium. Genetics and immunology explain Turner syndrome, the FMR1 premutation, and autoimmune oophoritis. Microbiology supplies the tubal scarring of pelvic inflammatory disease, and pathology links unopposed estrogen to hyperplasia and endometrioid carcinoma.

The limits of this framework matter. Hormone values fluctuate, especially in perimenopause and POI, so a single FSH can mislead, and PCOS does not fit neatly into the high or low gonadotropin categories because it is a disorder of feedback timing rather than of output. Low estrogen and unopposed estrogen are opposite problems with opposite risks: bone loss and cardiovascular risk in the first, endometrial hyperplasia in the second. Deciding which one a patient has is often the key step in a board question.

summary: Primary amenorrhea is no menarche by 15, or by 13 without breast development; secondary is 3 months without menses after regular cycles, and pregnancy is its most common cause.
Breast development shows past estrogen and a uterus shows Mullerian development; together they sort primary amenorrhea.

High FSH with low estradiol localizes amenorrhea to the ovary; low FSH, LH, and estradiol localize it to the hypothalamus or pituitary; normal hormones with no bleeding suggest an outflow defect such as Asherman syndrome.
Prolactin and the high TRH of primary hypothyroidism suppress GnRH pulses, so TSH and prolactin are part of every amenorrhea panel.
Anovulation means no corpus luteum and no progesterone; when estrogen is present, unopposed estrogen causes irregular heavy bleeding, hyperplasia, and endometrioid carcinoma risk.
AUB-O is asynchronous estrogen breakthrough shedding without secretory change, diagnosed after structural PALM causes and coagulopathy are excluded.
Menopause begins with falling inhibin B and early FSH rise; loss of estradiol causes vasomotor symptoms, vaginal atrophy, osteoporosis, and higher cardiovascular risk.
Primary ovarian insufficiency is the menopausal hormone profile before 40, caused by Turner syndrome, FMR1 premutation, autoimmunity, or gonadotoxic therapy, and is often intermittent.
Raised testosterone with normal DHEA-S points to the ovary; raised DHEA-S points to the adrenal; rapid virilization suggests a tumor.
Primary dysmenorrhea is prostaglandin-driven hypercontractility and ischemia after progesterone withdrawal; infertility is ovulatory, tubal, or uterine according to which step of conception fails.
